title: The Suffering and Praise
overview: Psalm 22 is a profound and poignant psalm of lament and trust attributed to David. It vividly portrays the anguish of abandonment and intense suffering, yet moves toward confident praise and hope in God's deliverance. This chapter is significant for its prophetic imagery that Christians recognize as foreshadowing the crucifixion of Christ, especially in its detailed descriptions of suffering and mockery. The psalm transitions from a cry of despair to a declaration of God’s faithfulness and ultimate reign, emphasizing the themes of divine presence in suffering and the future gathering of all nations to worship the Lord. It holds a crucial place in the Psalter as a bridge between lament and praise, illustrating the believer’s journey through trial to triumph.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: The Cry of Abandonment.** The psalm opens with a heartfelt plea expressing a sense of divine forsaking and unanswered prayer, yet acknowledges God's holiness and past faithfulness to Israel’s ancestors.

**Verses 6-18: The Description of Suffering.** The psalmist describes his extreme physical and emotional distress, including mockery by enemies and vivid imagery of being surrounded and pierced, which Christians see as prophetic of Christ’s crucifixion.

**Verses 19-21: The Plea for Deliverance.** The psalmist urgently appeals to God for rescue from death and hostile forces, emphasizing trust in God’s power to save.

**Verses 22-31: The Declaration of Praise and Universal Worship.** The tone shifts to confident praise, promising to proclaim God’s name publicly and foretelling that all nations will worship the Lord, highlighting God’s sovereign kingdom and eternal righteousness.

keyVerses.text: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
keyVerses.significance: This opening verse expresses the depth of the psalmist’s anguish and sense of abandonment, a cry that Jesus famously echoed on the cross, linking this psalm to the Messiah’s suffering and highlighting the reality of divine forsaking in human experience.

keyVerses.text: For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
keyVerses.significance: This verse contains vivid imagery of violent attack and piercing, which Christians interpret as a prophetic description of the crucifixion wounds of Christ, underscoring the psalm’s messianic significance.

keyVerses.text: I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.
keyVerses.significance: Here the psalmist shifts from lament to public praise, demonstrating faith in God’s deliverance and the importance of communal worship and testimony in the life of the believer.

keyVerses.text: All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the universal scope of God’s kingdom and the future gathering of all peoples to worship Him, emphasizing the global and eternal reign of God.

characters.name: The Psalmist (David)
characters.description: The speaker of the psalm, traditionally King David, who expresses profound suffering, abandonment, and mockery but ultimately trusts in God’s deliverance and proclaims His praise.

characters.name: Enemies/Wicked Assembly
characters.description: Represent hostile forces surrounding and attacking the psalmist, mocking his trust in God and inflicting physical and emotional pain, symbolizing opposition to God’s people.

characters.name: God (The LORD)
characters.description: The holy and sovereign God who is both the object of the psalmist’s lament and the source of deliverance, strength, and ultimate reign over all nations.

themes.description: The psalm vividly portrays the experience of feeling forsaken by God, a theme that resonates deeply in the biblical narrative of human suffering and is fulfilled in the Messiah’s passion.
Despite intense suffering, the psalmist maintains trust in God’s past faithfulness and pleads for rescue, reflecting the biblical call to rely on God amid trials.
The detailed descriptions of piercing, mockery, and suffering are seen as prophetic foreshadowings of Christ’s crucifixion, linking Old Testament hope with New Testament fulfillment.
The psalm concludes with a vision of all nations worshiping God, emphasizing His eternal kingdom and the global scope of salvation history.

historicalContext: Psalm 22 is traditionally attributed to King David, placing its composition around the 10th century BC during the united monarchy of Israel. The psalm reflects the cultural context of ancient Israel, where lament psalms were common expressions of distress and trust in Yahweh. The imagery of bulls of Bashan and wild animals reflects the pastoral and agrarian environment of the region. Politically, Israel faced threats from surrounding nations, and the psalm’s references to hostile assemblies and enemies echo the real dangers faced by the people and their leaders. The practice of casting lots for garments was a known custom, later seen in the New Testament crucifixion narrative. Understanding these customs and geopolitical realities helps illuminate the psalm’s vivid language and its theological depth.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes the psalm’s messianic prophecy, seeing Christ’s suffering as the ultimate fulfillment of the psalmist’s lament and the basis for believers’ hope in God’s sovereign deliverance.

Dispensational interpreters often highlight the distinction between David’s personal suffering and the future fulfillment in Christ, viewing the psalm as both a historical lament and a prophetic revelation of the Messiah’s passion.

Early church fathers such as Augustine and Chrysostom interpreted Psalm 22 as a direct prophecy of Christ’s crucifixion, using the psalm in liturgy and preaching to reveal Jesus’ fulfillment of Old Testament suffering and victory.

crossReferences.connection: Jesus quotes Psalm 22:1 on the cross, expressing the fulfillment of the psalm’s opening cry of abandonment.
The soldiers casting lots for Jesus’ garments fulfills the imagery of Psalm 22:18.
The suffering servant’s pierced hands and feet in Isaiah complement the messianic suffering described in Psalm 22.
Paul references the universal worship of God by all nations, echoing Psalm 22:27-28.
The declaration of God’s name among brethren in Psalm 22:22 is applied to Christ’s ministry.

application: In times of personal suffering, believers can honestly cry out to God, knowing He hears and understands our pain.
Trust in God’s faithfulness by remembering His past deliverances and promises, even when immediate relief seems absent.
Use your trials as opportunities to publicly declare God’s name and testify to His sustaining power.
Recognize that suffering can have a redemptive purpose, connecting us to Christ’s own experience and strengthening our faith.
Live with the hope that God’s kingdom will extend to all nations, motivating evangelism and worship.
Approach prayer with both lament and praise, embracing the full range of human emotions before God.
conclusion: Psalm 22 stands as a timeless testimony to the reality of suffering, the experience of divine abandonment, and the power of steadfast faith. It bridges human anguish with divine sovereignty, culminating in a vision of universal worship and God’s eternal reign. For believers today, it offers both comfort in trials and a call to proclaim God’s name boldly. The psalm’s prophetic elements deepen its significance, revealing Christ’s fulfillment and inviting Christians to unite their sufferings with His redemptive work. Ultimately, Psalm 22 encourages a journey from despair to hope, from isolation to community, and from pain to praise.
timeline: c. 1000 BC - Reign of King David, United Monarchy of Israel

outline.heading: The Cry of Abandonment and Trust in God’s Holiness
outline.description: The psalmist begins with a desperate plea for help, feeling forsaken, yet acknowledges God’s holiness and recalls the faithfulness shown to Israel’s ancestors.

outline.heading: The Description of Intense Suffering and Mockery
outline.description: A vivid portrayal of physical pain, emotional distress, and scorn from enemies, including prophetic imagery of piercing and the dividing of garments.

outline.heading: Urgent Plea for Deliverance
outline.description: The psalmist implores God to rescue him from death and hostile forces, expressing confident dependence on divine intervention.

outline.heading: Public Declaration of Praise and Universal Worship
outline.description: The tone shifts to praise, with promises to proclaim God’s name publicly and a vision of all nations worshiping the Lord, affirming His eternal kingdom.
